doc.title: Ed Soph interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 9, 2024

title: Whether rhythm is innate
summary: Asked about natural ability, he says everyone has potential and describes the range among his 32 North Texas students each semester.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: When you went to the African-American church, did you get an impression that — not exactly sure how to phrase this, but it might have something to do with your years of teaching — that some people are born with an inherent sense — I’m not going to say a sense of rhythm, I’m going to say an ability to hear it and then react to it. And some people aren’t.

Well to one degree or another I think that if a person can march in time then — or speak in time, recite something in time — that then in some form or another they can express that gift physically. But where the breakdown comes, I know so many people, aspiring drummers, who have such an incredible passion for the instrument and for the music, but that passion and desire is not matched by physical ability. And when I was at North Texas I had 32 students per semester. And invariably over the years there were — at the top there was maybe two or three students who were naturals, who had the coordination that came naturally. And then there was a wide breadth of students in the middle that could either, depending upon the success of the teacher, could either continue to expand or remain where they were. And then at the bottom, and I shouldn’t say bottom, I mean this is more — let’s think of it that way — there were the people who would have given whatever they needed to give to play well. But for some reason just physically could not get it together. Either inability to hold sticks in a way that allowed the body to move freely — I mean there’s so many variables involved that to make a blanket statement that some people have it and some people don’t, I don’t know if I would agree with that. I think there’s levels, like there are with every other ability. Some people have great memories, some people have mediocre memories. Some people can recite poetry well, some people can’t. You know. So I think everybody has a potential. There’s so many elements that go into it. Exposure obviously at an early age, and then early teaching experiences, whether or not early teachers encourage the student to discover for him- or herself rather than the teacher being dictatorial and saying this is the right way, all the others are wrong. And I mean this just doesn’t go for improvised music, it goes for any kind of music. It’s the imagination that makes the musician.
